Lately, I've been interviewing AI Engineer candidates with 1–2 years of experience.

One thing surprised me.
Almost everyone can talk about RAG.
Almost everyone has built AI agents.

Most have used LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini.
But when the conversation moves beyond frameworks...
...that's where many interviews start to slow down.

I ask simple questions like:
"Why do embeddings work?"
"Why does chunk size affect retrieval?"
"Why does an attention mechanism matter?"
"What actually happens before an LLM generates the first token?"

The room usually goes quiet.
It made me realize something.
We're getting really good at building AI applications.

But we're slowly skipping the fundamentals that make those applications reliable.
AI tools can write code.
They can generate APIs.
They can even scaffold an entire project.

But they can't replace your understanding.
If retrieval quality drops...
If latency suddenly doubles...
If hallucinations increase...
If your AI agent gets stuck in a loop...

The solution isn't another framework.
It's understanding what's happening underneath.
Frameworks will change.
Models will change.
The fundamentals won't.

That's why, before every interview, I'd rather revise concepts like:
→ Transformers
→ Attention Mechanism
→ Embeddings
→ Tokenization
→ Vector Search
→ HTTP & APIs
→ System Design
→ Memory
→ Databases
→ Evaluation
→ Python fundamentals
These are the concepts that help you explain why something works, not just how to build it.

If you're preparing for AI Engineer interviews, don't spend all your time learning the next framework.
Spend some time strengthening the foundation that every framework is built on.

📌 Tehran, IRNA – First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref has emphasized the need for strengthening the people-centered approach to deal with the enemies, arguing that today’s war is not merely limited to an exchange of fire, but also a test of willpower, strategic calculations, and national resilience.

In a message marking Basij Week on Sunday, Aref referred to constant anti-Iran plots, asserting that the countermeasure to the enemy’s strategy of economic attrition and sowing internal chaos needs the simultaneous reinforcement of people-centered security, along with the growth of scientific and economic power.
​
Pointing to the occasion dedicated to Basij —an organization of volunteer forces — he described it as a commemoration of one of the most astute strategic calculations made by the founder of the Islamic Republic, Imam Khomeini, with an initiative to prioritize a people-centered approach to security and progress.
​
He continued by saying that the same approach, under the wise guidance of the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, transformed the structure of Iran’s national power against the hegemonic system.
​
According to him, the resilience and endurance of the Iranian nation, despite simultaneous military, economic, and security challenges posed by the hegemonic system, is the result of unparalleled popular capacity, embodied by the Basij volunteer forces.
​
Unlike conventional armies that rely solely on military hardware, the Basij has established a neighborhood-based network, thereby extending the country’s strategic depth from its physical borders into the very heart of society, Aref noted.
​
He further hailed the vigilant presence of the Basij within the public sphere, depriving the enemy of any opportunity to catch them off guard or sow insecurity, thus helping the Armed Forces to guarantee superiority on the battlefield.
​
Referring to the multi-dimensional war being launched by the United States, Aref said the global arrogance—having failed to break the will of the Iranian nation in direct military confrontation—has now resorted to economic attrition, cognitive warfare, and the disruption of public tranquility.
​
At the end, while congratulating all self-sacrificing Basij members on this auspicious week, the Vice President emphasized that, following the path of the martyred Imam and the guidance from the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, the strategy of an "ever-stronger Iran" stands as the definitive agenda for the government and relevant institutions.

Could Bitcoin’s quantum-security upgrade take years?

About 7.12 million BTC are exposed through public keys. They could become vulnerable if quantum computers advance enough to break Bitcoin’s cryptography, a threshold not yet reached.

Leo Fan says securing the network and migrating funds may take longer than expected. Bridges, custodians and wallet providers will also need coordinated upgrades, while moving exposed funds at scale adds complexity.

Developers are debating migration strategies, and custodians have started testing quantum-resistant upgrades. With millions of coins across multiple infrastructure layers and no central coordinator, a rapid transition appears unlikely.
